# Executable Action Planning

## Operational definition

An action plan specifies a recognizable behavior, an opportunity or context,
a starting condition and enough scope to identify completion. It turns an
intention into an action that can be attempted under real constraints.

## What this concept does not mean

It is not a complete wish list, a schedule with no margin or a contingency plan
for every obstacle. Specificity cannot compensate for missing time, skill,
materials, access or authority.

## Main mechanisms

Specifying the behavior and opportunity reduces ambiguity between intending and
starting. A duration or scope boundary limits planning from expanding into an
unbounded task. Feasibility checks expose conflicts before execution.

## Evidence summary

BCTTv1 defines action planning as detailed planning of behavioral performance,
including at least one contextual element. A meta-review of self-regulation
interventions found variable support for planning and related components across
behaviors and populations; the component is not uniformly effective.

## Evidence mapping

- Action planning includes detailed planning of context and behavioral performance: `src-bcttv1-2013` (`canonical_framework`).
- Self-regulation components did not show consistent effectiveness across all reviewed domains: `src-self-regulation-2020` (`systematic_review`).

## Relevant signals

A clear intention is paired with “when I can”; the task has no recognizable
first action; a calendar block conflicts with existing commitments; or planned
scope is larger than the available opportunity.

## Alternative explanations

Non-execution may reflect insufficient ability, strong aversiveness, an imposed
goal, environmental barriers or inadequate capacity. Adding detail does not
resolve those conditions.

## Information needed

The target behavior, minimum useful scope, real opportunity, fixed commitments,
materials, dependencies, travel and available margin.

## Practical implications

Use action planning when intention and control are present but execution is
underspecified. Prefer a contingency concept when a recurring obstacle, rather
than the normal opportunity, determines the response.

## Limitations

Detailed plans can fail in unpredictable routines and can themselves become
additional work. Precision should remain proportional to the decision.

## Sources

`src-bcttv1-2013`; `src-self-regulation-2020`.

# Observable Behavior

## Operational definition

An observable-behavior description replaces a global judgment about a person
with an account that another observer could recognize: the action or non-action,
its context, frequency or duration when relevant, and its near consequence. The
unit of analysis is an episode, not a personality trait.

## What this concept does not mean

It does not deny emotions, reduce a person to metrics or require exhaustive
tracking. A precise description also does not establish why the behavior
occurred or what function it served.

## Main mechanisms

Operational description makes the target and context explicit. This permits
different explanations—opportunity, skill, energy, clarity, access, safety or
priority—to remain distinguishable instead of being collapsed into a moral
label.

## Evidence summary

BCTO and BCTTv1 provide vocabularies for specifying observable, replicable
intervention content. They are descriptive frameworks. They are not causal
tests, diagnostic instruments or evidence that observing a behavior will by
itself change it.

## Evidence mapping

- BCTO defines behavior change techniques as observable, replicable intervention components: `src-bcto-2024` (`canonical_framework`).
- BCTTv1 standardizes descriptions of intervention content: `src-bcttv1-2013` (`canonical_framework`).

## Relevant signals

The available account consists mainly of labels such as lazy, weak,
undisciplined or incapable; an intention is reported without the moment of
execution; or competing explanations depend on different episodes.

## Alternative explanations

The same non-action may reflect insufficient time, knowledge, energy, access or
priority. It may also be a reasonable response to risk or changing conditions.

## Information needed

A recent episode, the intended action, what occurred instead, the context when
it changes interpretation, and the immediate consequence. Frequency is needed
only when the decision depends on a repeated pattern.

## Practical implications

Use the smallest episode description that can discriminate the relevant
alternatives. Missing records remain missing data; they are not evidence that a
failure occurred.

## Limitations

Reports may omit context or be affected by recall. Observability improves
description, not completeness, causality or clinical validity.

## Sources

`src-bcto-2024`; `src-bcttv1-2013`.

# Chosen, Internalized and Imposed Goals

## Operational definition

Goal autonomy distinguishes goals a person endorses from goals experienced
mainly as external pressure. Internalization can be partial: a required activity
may contain personally valued reasons without becoming intrinsically enjoyable.

## What this concept does not mean

It does not reduce motivation to an intrinsic-versus-extrinsic binary, imply
that obligations are unreal, or require manufacturing enthusiasm for every
goal. External consequences and duties can remain important facts.

## Main mechanisms

Perceived choice, competence and relatedness are proposed to support more
self-determined regulation. Pressure, unclear value and low perceived capacity
can produce different patterns even when outward behavior looks similar.

## Evidence summary

A meta-analysis of randomized health-behavior trials found small average effects
for self-determination-theory interventions and reported evidence consistent
with theoretically specified mediation, alongside publication and small-sample
bias. A separate review linked need-supportive intervention strategies with
autonomy support, need satisfaction and motivation; individual strategies had
limited independent associations. These aggregate findings do not establish why
one person rejects or maintains a specific goal.

## Evidence mapping

- Self-determination-theory interventions showed aggregate effects across randomized trials: `src-sdt-rct-2020` (`meta_analysis`).
- Need-supportive strategies were associated with autonomy support, need satisfaction and motivation across interventions: `src-sdt-techniques-2019` (`meta_analysis`).

## Relevant signals

The person says the goal belongs to someone else, reports pressure as the main
reason for action, no longer sees value in the objective, or wants to stop
despite an otherwise feasible plan.

## Alternative explanations

Apparent low motivation may reflect insufficient time, sleep, skill, access,
pain, unclear requirements or an unrealistic plan. Refusing one strategy does
not prove rejection of the underlying goal.

## Information needed

Who established the goal, actual consequences of refusal, personally endorsed
value, available choice, possibilities for negotiation and costs to the person
and others.

## Practical implications

Separate non-negotiable constraints from genuine choice. The relevant decision
may be to abandon the objective, change its reason or scope, or revise the plan
while preserving a personally valued outcome.

## Limitations

This framework does not adjudicate legal, employment, educational or care
obligations. Aggregate intervention effects should not be presented as a causal
explanation for an individual's motivation.

## Sources

`src-sdt-rct-2020`; `src-sdt-techniques-2019`.

# Goal Review

## Operational definition

Goal review compares the stated objective, behavior performed, progress,
current cost and changed conditions in order to choose explicitly among keeping,
replanning, rescheduling, replacing, pausing or abandoning the goal.

## What this concept does not mean

Review is not automatic reduction whenever discomfort appears, preservation of
a goal at any cost, or treating a change in plan as abandonment of the desired
outcome.

## Main mechanisms

Separating outcome, controllable behavior, deadline, measurement and conditions
locates the mismatch. A person can execute the planned behavior without seeing
the expected progress, or make progress at a cost that changes the decision.

## Evidence summary

BCTTv1 distinguishes review of behavioral goals from review of outcome goals.
A meta-analysis by Epton and colleagues found a small positive average effect
of goal setting across behaviors, with meaningful heterogeneity and moderators.
This supports calibrated review, not a universal prescription.

## Evidence mapping

- BCTTv1 distinguishes review of behavioral and outcome goals in light of performance: `src-bcttv1-2013` (`canonical_framework`).
- Goal setting had a small positive average effect, with heterogeneity and moderators: `src-goal-setting-2017` (`meta_analysis`).

## Relevant signals

Deadlines are repeatedly moved without new information; execution is adequate
but progress is not; progress requires disproportionate cost; the goal was
externally imposed; or work, health, care duties or resources changed.

## Alternative explanations

Low apparent progress may result from a poor measure, an incompatible plan, a
short observation window, third-party dependencies or a change in priority.

## Information needed

The current objective, controllable behavior, planned versus performed action,
progress measure, cost, current importance, changed constraints and the
appropriate decision horizon.

## Practical implications

Classify the mismatch before changing the goal. Record which element changed
and what observation would justify the next review.

## Limitations

Average effects do not determine the best adjustment for one person. Values,
resources and obligations can justify decisions that do not maximize measured
performance.

## Sources

`src-bcttv1-2013`; `src-goal-setting-2017`.

# Habit Formation and Automaticity

## Operational definition

Habit formation is the gradual increase in the automaticity of a response
through repetition in contexts that provide recurring cues. Repetition can
produce a functional routine before the response feels automatic.

## What this concept does not mean

There is no universal 21-day or 66-day deadline. Habit is not synonymous with
discipline, perfect frequency, an activity placed on a calendar or every complex
routine performed regularly.

## Main mechanisms

Repeated pairing of a discriminable context with a sufficiently stable response
can reduce reliance on deliberate remembering. Simpler responses and recurring
opportunities are easier to repeat consistently than complex, variable tasks.

## Evidence summary

Lally and colleagues observed asymptotic automaticity curves and substantial
variation across 96 participants. A 2024 systematic review reported medians
around two months in a small evidence base, larger means and wide individual
ranges; many studies had high risk of bias. Context stability predicted
automaticity and repetition in two longitudinal datasets, but does not guarantee
maintenance.

## Evidence mapping

- Automaticity increased asymptotically and varied across people and behaviors: `src-habit-lally-2010` (`observational_study`).
- Formation time was widely variable in a limited, heterogeneous evidence base: `src-habit-review-2024` (`systematic_review`).
- More stable contexts predicted automaticity and repetition across one manipulated and one observational longitudinal dataset: `src-context-stability-2022` (`mixed_experimental_and_observational_longitudinal_studies`).

## Relevant signals

The action still depends on deliberate reminders, occurs in substantially
different contexts, or is too complex to function as one repeatable response.

## Alternative explanations

Forgetting may indicate an inadequate reminder rather than absent learning. Low
repetition may reflect few opportunities. A complex activity can continue to
require planning even after months of successful performance.

## Information needed

The specific response, candidate cue, actual opportunity and frequency,
complexity, weeks observed and a measure that distinguishes frequency from
subjective automaticity.

## Practical implications

Stabilizing a cue or simplifying the response may be useful when opportunities
recur. Automaticity is not required for a routine to be successful.

## Limitations

Much of the evidence relies on self-report and a limited set of health
behaviors. Findings should not be used to alter prescribed treatment or promise
a formation deadline.

## Sources

`src-habit-lally-2010`; `src-habit-review-2024`; `src-context-stability-2022`.

# Implementation Intentions

## Operational definition

An implementation intention links a discriminable situation to an available
response: if situation Y occurs, then action X will follow. It can support
starting, protecting or resuming action when a recurring obstacle appears.

## What this concept does not mean

It is not an ordinary schedule, positive thinking or an exhaustive list of
exceptions. It presupposes an endorsed goal and a response that is feasible in
the specified situation.

## Main mechanisms

The conditional link makes a relevant cue easier to recognize and preselects a
response before the obstacle occurs. This addresses execution without assuming
that strengthening intention alone will produce equivalent behavioral change.

## Evidence summary

Gollwitzer and Sheeran synthesized 94 tests and reported a positive average
effect of implementation intentions on goal attainment. Webb and Sheeran found
that experimentally changed intentions produced smaller changes in behavior,
supporting a distinction between wanting and executing. Effects vary by goal,
context and implementation quality.

## Evidence mapping

- If-then plans specifying when, where or how to act showed a positive aggregate effect on goal attainment: `src-ii-2006` (`meta_analysis`).
- Changes in intention were not fully translated into behavioral changes: `src-intention-behavior-2006` (`meta_analysis`).

## Relevant signals

The same recognizable event repeatedly precedes failure to start, interruption
or failure to resume, such as a delayed meeting, a specific distraction or a
return from travel.

## Alternative explanations

A rare, vague or uncontrollable obstacle may require capacity reserve,
negotiation or revision of the goal rather than a conditional response.

## Information needed

The endorsed goal, observable trigger, trigger frequency, control over the
response, response cost and any conflict with safety or fixed obligations.

## Practical implications

Prefer one high-value contingency over many hypothetical rules. Evaluate the
plan only after the trigger actually occurs; absence of the trigger is not
failure.

## Limitations

Aggregate effects do not guarantee individual benefit. Rigid contingencies can
be ineffective when opportunities and constraints change continuously.

## Sources

`src-ii-2006`; `src-intention-behavior-2006`.

# Physical Activity Consistency Without Individual Prescription

## Operational definition

Physical-activity consistency is repeated participation compatible with a
person's context and stated capacity. Population guidelines describe volume,
intensity and strengthening targets; they do not prescribe an individualized
starting load or progression.

## What this concept does not mean

Consistency does not require daily training, compensating for missed sessions
or continuing through pain. A population target such as 150 minutes is not a
mandatory starting point for every individual.

## Main mechanisms

Distributing feasible opportunities can support repeated participation while
preserving recovery. Population guidance provides a reference for overall
health behavior, not an algorithm for exercise programming.

## Evidence summary

WHO provides physical-activity and sedentary-behavior recommendations by age
group and emphasizes that some activity is better than none. CDC presents the
general adult reference of at least 150 minutes of moderate-intensity activity
per week plus strengthening, together with cautions for specific conditions and
vigorous activity after inactivity.

## Evidence mapping

- WHO provides population recommendations for frequency, intensity and duration by age group: `src-who-pa-2020` (`institutional_guideline`).
- CDC presents adult weekly guidance and circumstances requiring professional input: `src-cdc-pa-adults` (`institutional_guideline`).

## Relevant signals

The user asks how to organize an already chosen activity, treats the weekly
reference as an all-or-nothing threshold, or proposes compensating for a missed
session by abruptly increasing volume.

## Alternative explanations

Low frequency may reflect travel, cost, care duties, preference, weather,
access or recovery. It does not establish low motivation.

## Information needed

The intended activity, current experience, available time, environment,
equipment and any known professional guidance. Clinical or critical information
is evaluated outside RAG by the Security Gate.

## Practical implications

Use guidelines as context while organizing feasible opportunities. Do not infer
individual readiness, prescribe load or technique, or define clinical
progression from completion data.

## Limitations

Population guidelines do not assess individual risk or replace qualified
exercise, rehabilitation or medical professionals.

## Sources

`src-who-pa-2020`; `src-cdc-pa-adults`.

# Functional Pattern of Procrastination

## Operational definition

Procrastination is voluntary delay despite expecting the delay to make the
outcome worse. A functional pattern describes the antecedent, alternative
action, immediate payoff and later cost before selecting an explanation.

## What this concept does not mean

Not every delay is procrastination. Missing time, information, access, ability,
decision authority or safety can make postponement reasonable or unavoidable.
The concept is not a personality label or clinical diagnosis.

## Main mechanisms

Task aversiveness, delayed rewards, low expectancy and access to more immediate
rewards can shift behavior away from an intended task. These are candidate
mechanisms; an episode-level description is needed to distinguish them from
practical constraints.

## Evidence summary

Steel's meta-analysis reported associations between procrastination and factors
including task aversiveness, reward delay, self-efficacy and impulsiveness. A
systematic review of psychological treatments found a small, heterogeneous
overall benefit across few trials. Neither synthesis identifies one universal
cause or intervention.

## Evidence mapping

- Task aversiveness, delay, self-efficacy and impulsiveness showed relevant aggregate associations: `src-procrastination-steel-2007` (`meta_analysis`).
- Psychological treatments showed a small heterogeneous benefit in a limited trial base: `src-procrastination-treatment-2018` (`systematic_review`).

## Relevant signals

The person performs peripheral preparation, switches to a more immediately
rewarding activity or waits for deadline pressure while still intending to do
the task.

## Alternative explanations

Strategic delay, a competing priority, incomplete instructions, exhaustion,
pain, an imposed goal or dependency on another person can produce similar
outward delay.

## Information needed

The chosen task, deadline, a recent episode, the alternative action, its
immediate consequence, expected later cost, available skill and resources.

## Practical implications

Match any strategy to the best-supported episode mechanism and identify an
observation that would contradict that explanation. Avoid applying a generic
anti-procrastination list.

## Limitations

Correlates are not individual causes. Persistent or disabling distress is
outside the scope of a routine-coaching explanation.

## Sources

`src-procrastination-steel-2007`; `src-procrastination-treatment-2018`.

# Retrieval Practice with Feedback

## Operational definition

Retrieval practice requires attempting to produce an answer from memory before
consulting the solution, followed by feedback or correction. The target is
retention and later use, not familiarity while looking at the material.

## What this concept does not mean

It is not merely rereading a question and answer, copying notes or taking a
high-stakes test. Repeated retrieval without corrective feedback can preserve
errors, and retrieval cannot replace initial comprehension.

## Main mechanisms

Effortful access strengthens later accessibility and reveals what cannot yet be
produced. Feedback corrects errors and distinguishes a retrieval problem from a
gap in prior understanding.

## Evidence summary

Dunlosky and colleagues rated practice testing as a high-utility learning
technique across conditions. A later classroom meta-analysis found a positive
average effect of retrieval practice, with variation by design, feedback,
material and educational context.

## Evidence mapping

- A broad evidence review rated practice testing as high utility across learning conditions: `src-learning-dunlosky-2013` (`systematic_review`).
- Classroom retrieval practice showed a positive aggregate effect with moderators and heterogeneity: `src-retrieval-meta-2021` (`meta_analysis`).

## Relevant signals

Study consists mainly of rereading or highlighting; material feels familiar but
cannot be produced without cues; or errors remain uncorrected after practice.

## Alternative explanations

Poor retrieval may reflect inadequate initial comprehension, ambiguous prompts,
missing prerequisite knowledge or a mismatch between practice and the required
application format.

## Information needed

The learning objective, material, prior understanding, expected response format,
availability and timing of correct feedback, delay until use and recurring
errors.

## Practical implications

Select prompts that require the form of knowledge needed later. Attempt an
answer before checking, correct it promptly and revisit errors rather than
counting exposure alone.

## Limitations

Effect size varies across learners, materials and settings. Retrieval practice
is not a complete curriculum and does not guarantee transfer to a substantially
different task.

## Sources

`src-learning-dunlosky-2013`; `src-retrieval-meta-2021`.

# Decision-Oriented Self-Monitoring

## Operational definition

Self-monitoring is recording a defined behavior or outcome to support a later
decision. A usable record specifies the variable, collection frequency,
observation period and the decision that the information may change.

## What this concept does not mean

It is not continuous surveillance, a score of personal worth or evidence that
an unrecorded event failed to occur. More variables and longer collection do not
automatically improve inference.

## Main mechanisms

Consistent observation can make discrepancies, context and change visible.
Defining the decision first limits collection burden and reduces the temptation
to interpret every fluctuation after the fact.

## Evidence summary

BCTTv1 defines self-monitoring of behavior and outcomes as separate techniques.
A meta-review of self-regulation interventions found variable effectiveness
across domains and components. Monitoring is therefore a way to obtain decision
data, not a guarantee of behavior change.

## Evidence mapping

- BCTTv1 distinguishes self-monitoring of behavior from self-monitoring of outcomes: `src-bcttv1-2013` (`canonical_framework`).
- Self-regulation components showed variable effectiveness across reviewed behaviors and populations: `src-self-regulation-2020` (`systematic_review`).

## Relevant signals

A decision depends on a pattern that is not yet observable; conclusions are
being drawn from incomplete coverage; or collection burden exceeds the value of
the possible decision.

## Alternative explanations

A change in the record may reflect missing entries, changed opportunities,
measurement drift or ordinary fluctuation rather than a behavioral change.

## Information needed

The decision question, observable variable, collection method, expected
coverage, burden, privacy implications, observation window and handling of
missing data.

## Practical implications

Collect the minimum variable for the shortest window that can distinguish the
relevant alternatives. Report coverage and missingness with the result.

## Limitations

Self-report and automated logs can both be incomplete. Observational patterns
do not establish causality, and intrusive collection can create privacy or
behavioral costs.

## Sources

`src-bcttv1-2013`; `src-self-regulation-2020`.

# Sleep Duration as Population Guidance

## Operational definition

Sleep duration is time actually slept over a 24-hour period. Population
recommendations provide reference ranges by age; individual need and impact also
depend on health, regularity, quality and sleep opportunity.

## What this concept does not mean

A population range is not an individual prescription or a diagnosis based on
one night. Time in bed is not necessarily time asleep, and duration alone does
not establish sleep quality.

## Main mechanisms

Regular sleep opportunity supports multiple health and functioning outcomes.
Comparing a sustained pattern with an age-appropriate reference can identify
when routine optimization should give way to a different assessment, but it
cannot identify a cause.

## Evidence summary

The American Academy of Sleep Medicine and Sleep Research Society recommend
that healthy adults sleep seven or more hours regularly to promote optimal
health. The National Sleep Foundation provides age-specific ranges based on a
multidisciplinary consensus process. Neither source supports routinely reducing
sleep to increase productivity.

## Evidence mapping

- AASM/SRS consensus recommends seven or more hours of regular sleep for healthy adults: `src-sleep-aasm-2015` (`institutional_guideline`).
- A multidisciplinary panel established recommended ranges by age group: `src-sleep-nsf-2015` (`institutional_guideline`).

## Relevant signals

Habitual sleep is substantially below the population reference, daytime
sleepiness affects functioning, or duration appears adequate while impairment
persists.

## Alternative explanations

A short measurement may be an isolated event or inaccurate estimate. Tiredness
has causes other than sleep duration, and adequate duration does not exclude
fragmented or poor-quality sleep.

## Information needed

Age, typical duration and window, duration of the pattern, daytime impact, shift
work, fragmentation and known health or medication context. Critical risk is
handled by the Security Gate before retrieval.

## Practical implications

Use the range only as a population reference. Routine planning may preserve
sleep opportunity, but causal explanation, diagnosis and treatment remain
outside this concept.

## Limitations

Consensus ranges do not measure individual need. Shift work, symptoms,
conditions and medication can require professional assessment.

## Sources

`src-sleep-aasm-2015`; `src-sleep-nsf-2015`.

# Spaced Practice

## Operational definition

Spaced practice distributes contact with and retrieval of material across more
than one session separated in time. The interval allows some forgetting while
retaining a realistic chance of successful reconstruction and correction.

## What this concept does not mean

It is not postponing first contact, applying a universal interval formula or
splitting the same total time without later retrieval. A schedule alone does not
show that learning was retained.

## Main mechanisms

Returning after a delay requires reconstruction rather than continuous
familiarity. Performance after different intervals provides information for
adjusting subsequent spacing by item difficulty and the required retention
horizon.

## Evidence summary

Dunlosky and colleagues rated distributed practice as high utility. A 2024
systematic review in health-professions education generally supported spaced
learning while reporting heterogeneous designs and outcomes. The optimal
interval depends on material, learner and how long knowledge must be retained.

## Evidence mapping

- A broad evidence review rated distributed practice as high utility: `src-learning-dunlosky-2013` (`systematic_review`).
- A recent health-professions review generally supported spaced learning but found heterogeneous implementation and outcomes: `src-spacing-review-2024` (`systematic_review`).

## Relevant signals

Most study is concentrated immediately before use; initial performance is good
but later recall is poor; or a large volume is reviewed once without later
retrieval.

## Alternative explanations

Low later performance may reflect weak initial comprehension. Spacing material
that was not understood can repeat confusion rather than resolve it.

## Information needed

The date and form of later use, material units, current understanding, available
opportunities, retrieval difficulty after intervals and total time constraints.

## Practical implications

Schedule at least two later retrieval opportunities when the horizon permits.
Shorten intervals for items that cannot yet be reconstructed and lengthen them
when retrieval is consistently successful.

## Limitations

The recent review is concentrated in health-professions education. No single
interval is optimal across materials, learners or retention horizons.

## Sources

`src-learning-dunlosky-2013`; `src-spacing-review-2024`.

# Standards Block Completion or Submission

## Activation criteria

Revision, delay or non-submission is linked to a quality standard or anticipated
evaluation, and at least one version already exists or could be produced.

## Similar situations that should not activate this playbook

Do not activate when the work objectively misses an explicit requirement, the
user lacks a prerequisite skill, or the user has decided not to submit.

## Possible explanations

The completion criterion may be undefined, the cost of a minor error may be
overestimated, exposure to evaluation may be avoided, or an external standard
may be genuinely strict.

## Missing information

Explicit requirements, actual consequences of error, who evaluates the work,
the versions already produced, the remaining skill gap and the deadline.

## Response objective

Distinguish required quality from revision that no longer changes the relevant
outcome, then define a verifiable completion or learning decision.

## Decision path

- If requirements are explicit and unmet, convert them into a finite checklist.
- If requirements are met but completion is undefined, set a completion criterion and revision boundary.
- If a specific skill is missing, practice that component before requiring submission.
- If the user does not intend to submit, review the goal rather than forcing completion.

## Candidate strategies

Requirement checklist, completion criterion, revision limit, graded exposure to
feedback and focused skill practice.

## Conditions for selecting each strategy

Use a checklist for external criteria, a revision limit when later passes produce
no relevant change, graded exposure when evaluation is the observed barrier and
focused practice when errors identify a concrete skill gap.

## When to ask a question

Ask when the distinction between an unmet requirement and an undefined standard
is not available from the user's description.

## When to respond directly

Respond directly when the stated requirements and repeated revision cycles make
the applicable branch clear.

## What to avoid

Do not recommend accepting any quality level, diagnose perfectionism, or lower a
real professional, academic or safety requirement.

## Suggested next step

Choose the next verifiable boundary: complete one unmet requirement, stop after
a defined review pass, or request targeted feedback.

## Related knowledge

`evaluative-avoidance`; `procrastination-pattern`; `goal-difficulty`; `goal-review`.

# User Cannot Start a Chosen Task

## Activation criteria

The user has chosen a task and describes a recent opportunity in which the
first task-producing action did not occur.

## Similar situations that should not activate this playbook

Do not activate when there was no real opportunity, the task lacks basic
instructions, the user rejects the goal, or tiredness is the stated barrier.

## Possible explanations

The first action may be ambiguous; a prerequisite skill or resource may be
missing; preparation may provide an easier immediate reward; the task may feel
aversive; or anticipated evaluation may block exposure.

## Missing information

The most recent start opportunity, what the user did instead, whether the first
action was known, and whether time, materials and prerequisite skill were
available.

## Response objective

Identify the most plausible start barrier and select one matching intervention,
without treating non-initiation as a character defect.

## Decision path

- If the first action is unknown, define one observable task-producing action.
- If a prerequisite is missing, resolve instruction, example, access or help before planning execution.
- If preparation repeatedly replaces production, place a boundary around preparation and begin with an output.
- If the action is beyond demonstrated capacity, select a smaller graded component with an explicit progression condition.
- If immediate relief or a nearer reward repeatedly wins, bring a task consequence or feedback point closer rather than adding task detail.
- If anticipated evaluation is the barrier, define the required standard and a proportionate exposure to real feedback.
- If the same environmental obstacle recurs, change that observed cue or access step rather than redesigning the whole task.
- If the goal is not endorsed, leave this playbook and evaluate goal autonomy.

## Candidate strategies

Action planning, prerequisite resolution, graded task structure, consequence or
feedback proximity, fit-for-purpose exposure and environmental-friction change.

## Conditions for selecting each strategy

Use action planning for ambiguity, graded structure for a capacity gap, resource
preparation for a concrete missing dependency, reward-timing change for a
repeated immediate-payoff pattern, exposure for evaluative avoidance and an
environmental change only when the same barrier is observed across episodes.

## When to ask a question

Ask one question when the answer distinguishes two different branches, usually
about the latest start opportunity or the first known action.

## When to respond directly

Respond directly when task, antecedent, substitute action and missing condition
are already explicit.

## What to avoid

Do not provide a generic productivity list, assume low motivation, or reduce a
task whose missing prerequisite has not been addressed.

## Suggested next step

Define or prepare the single first task-producing action that corresponds to
the supported branch.

## Related knowledge

`procrastination-pattern`; `observable-behavior`; `action-planning`; `task-aversiveness`;
`temporal-discounting`; `evaluative-avoidance`;
`environmental-cues-and-friction`.

# User Has an Irregular Schedule

## Activation criteria

Clock times vary, but the user can identify recurring events, minimum windows or
a small number of day types.

## Similar situations that should not activate this playbook

Do not activate when total commitments already exceed capacity or when no
relevant event or window is under the user's control.

## Possible explanations

Clock-based planning may be incompatible with the schedule. Event anchors,
rules by day type or delayed planning after a roster arrives may fit the actual
opportunity structure better.

## Missing information

Recurring events, notice period for the schedule, minimum usable windows,
travel, fixed duties and how often each day type occurs.

## Response objective

Create one feasible planning rule that tolerates real variation instead of
simulating a fixed weekly schedule.

## Decision path

- If one recurring event reliably occurs, attach a defined action to that event.
- If there are a few recognizable day types, define one priority rule per type.
- If the schedule arrives late, defer time selection while preserving priority, materials and minimum scope.
- If no controllable opportunity exists, move to capacity or goal review rather than creating a fictional anchor.

## Candidate strategies

Event-based action plan, implementation intention, day-type plan and prepared
task menu by available window.

## Conditions for selecting each strategy

Use an event anchor when the event is stable, an if-then rule for a recurring
obstacle, day-type planning for a small set of patterns and a task menu when only
window length becomes known in advance.

## When to ask a question

Ask when the existence of a recurring event or recognizable day type determines
which planning form is feasible.

## When to respond directly

Respond directly when the event and action, or the day types and constraints,
are already explicit.

## What to avoid

Do not impose an identical daily time, create seven elaborate routines or treat
schedule variability as noncompliance.

## Suggested next step

Select one recurring event or day type and define the corresponding action and
completion boundary.

## Related knowledge

`action-planning`; `implementation-intentions`; `habit-formation`.

I work changing shifts
I cannot use a fixed time
every day has a different routine

# User Questions the Value or Ownership of a Goal

## Activation criteria

The user explicitly questions the value, ownership or continued desirability of
a goal.

## Similar situations that should not activate this playbook

Do not activate when the demonstrated barrier is insufficient time, missing
skill, unavailable resources or tiredness while the goal remains endorsed.

## Possible explanations

The goal may be imposed, may have lost value, may conflict with a higher
priority, or may still matter while its current cost or plan is unacceptable.

## Missing information

Who set the goal, the real consequences of refusing it, any personally endorsed
value, the available degree of choice and whether the user wants analysis,
options or simply acknowledgment.

## Response objective

Clarify the decision without manufacturing motivation or treating abandonment
as failure.

## Decision path

- If the goal is rejected and optional, consider ending or replacing it.
- If a real obligation exists, separate the required minimum from an idealized version.
- If the outcome remains valued but current cost is excessive, review scope, plan or deadline.
- If the user wants acknowledgment rather than options, do not continue into planning.

## Candidate strategies

Goal discontinuation, goal substitution, minimum-obligation definition, value
clarification and goal review.

## Conditions for selecting each strategy

Use discontinuation or substitution when choice is genuine, minimum-obligation
definition when consequences are fixed, and goal review when value remains but
the current arrangement is unsustainable.

## When to ask a question

Ask when the presence of a real obligation or personally endorsed value changes
the branch and is not yet known.

## When to respond directly

Respond directly when the user clearly rejects an optional goal or clearly
identifies an obligation and the desired form of help.

## What to avoid

Do not persuade, use theory to invalidate the decision, or assume every loss of
execution is a motivation problem.

## Suggested next step

Record the explicit choice: end, replace, define the required minimum or review
the plan for a still-valued outcome.

## Related knowledge

`goal-autonomy`; `goal-review`.

trigger_phrases: I have no motivation for this goal
this goal is for other people
I do not see the point anymore
I do not want this goal

# User Rejects a Suggestion

## Activation criteria

The user explicitly rejects a proposed technique, explanation or direction.
The rejection is the current conversational decision, not merely a weak signal.

## Similar situations that should not activate this playbook

A request for evidence, a clarifying question or uncertainty about implementation
is not necessarily rejection.

## Possible explanations

The suggestion may conflict with cost, prior experience, values, resources or a
conversational preference. The rejection itself is useful information and does
not indicate unwillingness to cooperate.

## Missing information

Whether the user wants to explain the mismatch, choose an alternative, continue
without advice or end the exchange.

## Response objective

Stop the rejected direction, incorporate any stated constraint and return
control without disguising the same suggestion as a new one.

## Decision path

- Stop presenting the rejected strategy.
- If the user gives a reason, treat it as a constraint for future options.
- If the user requests an alternative, offer at most one materially different route.
- If the user asks to stop or end, do so without another coaching question.

## Candidate strategies

Acknowledgment, constraint update, a genuinely different option, listening or
ending the exchange.

## Conditions for selecting each strategy

Use an alternative only after the user indicates that another option is wanted.
Use listening when advice is declined but continued conversation is invited;
end when the user requests it.

## When to ask a question

Ask only when the user remains open and the answer selects among a different
option, listening or ending.

## When to respond directly

Respond directly when the reason or request to stop is explicit.

## What to avoid

Do not defend the prior suggestion, cite evidence to win the objection, relabel
the same technique or interpret rejection as a character trait.

## Suggested next step

Apply the user's stated boundary and proceed only along the option they selected.

## Related knowledge

`goal-autonomy`; `observable-behavior`.

trigger_phrases: that does not work for me
I do not want to do that
I already tried this
stop insisting

# User Reports Insufficient Capacity

## Activation criteria

Known commitments and realistic durations exceed available windows, or two
priorities compete for the same limited resource.

## Similar situations that should not activate this playbook

Do not activate from postponement alone. Ambiguity, missing skill, non-endorsed
goals and tiredness require different decisions.

## Possible explanations

Demand may genuinely exceed capacity; duration may be underestimated; priority
may be implicit; or an obligation may require renegotiation with another person.

## Missing information

Fixed commitments, realistic durations, deadlines, consequences of delay and
which commitments can be removed, delegated, reduced or renegotiated.

## Response objective

Make the capacity conflict explicit and select a tradeoff instead of adding
productivity techniques to an impossible schedule.

## Decision path

- If total demand exceeds capacity, identify what must be removed, delegated, delayed or renegotiated.
- If two priorities conflict, compare their current consequences and select one explicitly.
- If duration is uncertain, observe one representative execution before rebuilding the schedule.
- If the goal has lost priority, review or pause it rather than repeatedly shrinking the task.

## Candidate strategies

Demand removal, delegation, deadline negotiation, priority selection, duration
sampling and goal review.

## Conditions for selecting each strategy

Use removal or negotiation for arithmetic overload, duration sampling when the
estimate drives the conflict, and goal review when the objective no longer
justifies its opportunity cost.

## When to ask a question

Ask when one missing duration, consequence or degree of control changes the
tradeoff.

## When to respond directly

Respond directly when incompatibility is already explicit and the remaining
decision is which commitment moves.

## What to avoid

Do not present optimization as creation of time, add an unprioritized task list
or assume that every obligation is negotiable.

## Suggested next step

Name one commitment to remove, move, delegate, renegotiate or protect, together
with the consequence of that choice.

## Related knowledge

`goal-review`; `action-planning`; `time-estimation`.

trigger_phrases: I do not have enough time
my schedule cannot fit everything
everything is a priority
my commitments overlap

# User Reports Tiredness or Short Sleep

## Activation criteria

After the Security Gate returns a noncritical result, the user links routine
execution to tiredness, short sleep or a temporary reduction in energy.

## Similar situations that should not activate this playbook

Do not label every resistance or loss of interest as tiredness. Do not use this
playbook when the Security Gate has selected a critical or clinical boundary.

## Possible explanations

The pattern may involve reduced sleep opportunity, shift work, workload,
temporary disruption or another cause that RAG cannot determine.

## Missing information

Whether the report is one episode or a sustained pattern, typical sleep
duration, schedule changes, functional impact and which commitments are
negotiable. The Security Gate owns all critical screening information.

## Response objective

Protect recovery and adjust negotiable routine demands without diagnosing the
cause or turning a population sleep range into an individual prescription.

## Decision path

- If this is an isolated noncritical disruption, reschedule or reduce a negotiable demand.
- If schedule structure repeatedly limits sleep opportunity, examine capacity and fixed commitments.
- If a sustained pattern causes impairment without a critical signal, keep coaching limited and identify appropriate external assessment.
- If the user asks for a medical cause or treatment change, do not continue with routine optimization.

## Candidate strategies

Protecting sleep opportunity, rescheduling a negotiable task, capacity review
and a boundary toward appropriate assessment.

## Conditions for selecting each strategy

Use rescheduling for an isolated disruption, capacity review for repeated
schedule conflict and an external-assessment boundary when the pattern persists
or the requested decision exceeds routine planning.

## When to ask a question

Ask only for noncritical information that changes the planning branch, such as
whether the pattern is isolated or recurrent and what can be moved.

## When to respond directly

Respond directly when the noncritical schedule conflict and negotiable demand
are already clear.

## What to avoid

Do not diagnose, recommend medication or supplements, prescribe an individual
sleep duration or optimize productivity by reducing sleep.

## Suggested next step

Protect the next realistic sleep opportunity or move one negotiable demand; if
the issue exceeds routine planning, stop at the appropriate boundary.

## Related knowledge

`sleep-duration`; `sleep-regularity`; `observable-behavior`; `goal-review`.

I have been sleeping less
I have no energy for my routine
tiredness is affecting my plans
